title: 5 days Upper Lower program review (Week 2)
summary: NH reviews week two of a viewer's (White Wolf's) upper/lower program, which is built around supersets and giant sets, calling it one of the best programs he has reviewed. Along the way he critiques the incline barbell bench, praises seal rows and the SSB, explains why the upper back can take huge volume, and suggests lowering the rep ranges.
claims: 4x8-11 is a good range for incline barbell bench; 6-10 is also an option if you stay at 4 sets
He dislikes incline barbell bench: most benches' inclines make it closer to a horizontal press than people realize, it over-recruits the front delt, and it has a higher injury rate than flat bench
Telling people to incline bench for upper chest is usually bad advice; those who do get upper chest from it usually get it from overhead pressing too
Supersetting a non-strength compound that supports another compound is fine; he does it too
He prefers chin-ups or pull-ups to lat pulldowns; pulldowns are fine only on a machine where the bar comes straight down over your head
10-12 reps is excellent for cable work, and you can go higher because mechanical breakdown is easy to prevent, keeping fatigue muscular
Barbell seal rows are among the best rows because they take the posterior chain and leg drive out and let you pull with a horizontal torso
Superset horizontal presses with horizontal pulls and vertical with vertical; they complement each other perfectly
Two sets is too few for hammer curls; do more sets with lower reps
Two-round giant sets give a big pump and quality tonnage while taxing the cardiovascular system, but they are not the best setup for progression
The safety squat bar is a game changer that every gym and home gym should have

The SSB squat is not like a front squat: a front squat feels like being pulled forward at the chest via thoracic extension, the SSB like being pushed forward at the mid-back; neither replaces the other
Splitting hip hinge volume between RDLs and glute-ham raises, which may hit different parts of the hamstrings, is a valid alternative to four sets of RDLs
The football bar puts the emphasis of the bench press on the triceps
Supersetting neutral-grip bench with neutral-grip pull-ups is synergy by definition: press and pull with the same grip
Bodyweight pull-ups can be done for max reps, but weighted pull-ups need a set rep range so progression can be tracked
Rep the Viking press so the first rep's effort matches the last; a first rep slower than the rest means the setup puts you in a weak, injury-prone position
Don't deadlift your T-bar rows: some leg drive is fine, but without elbow flexion you are not training the back
Keep cable fly weight low because the shoulders can get hurt getting into position
You can never do enough rear delt work: they burn out muscularly before the structure is at risk, and once sore they are useless for days, so they need endurance to grow
Dumbbell incline bench beats barbell because you can tuck and adjust the elbow angle and spare the shoulders
12-15 on seal rows may be too high; lowering it keeps the intensity relevant
The upper back is the most underdeveloped body part in natural bodybuilders; once accustomed it can take insane volume and tonnage and grows from it
To bring up traps, add shrugs at multiple torso angles
Never apply body part split logic to the core: train it every day with isolation, contraction, stretching and isometrics
Many people who say they run upper/lower actually run a body part split, which he considers the best type of program
Lowering rep ranges by about 12-20% across the board would raise intensity
A strength week alternating with a volume week of similar tonnage is a terrible way to program; both volume and intensity need to exist every week
Two slightly different weeks repeated in a cycle are fine because each gets enough frequency and the variety keeps training fresh
The program would benefit from wrist curls, more long-head triceps work and more intense biceps work
exercises: closer to horizontal than thought, over-recruits front delt, higher injury rate
bar directly above head, not in front
acceptable only on a good machine; chin-ups preferred
isolates upper back, removes posterior chain
free squat, as low as you can
heavy posterior chain recruitment; distinct from front squat
triceps emphasis; pairs with neutral-grip pull-ups
rep it so the first rep matches the last
avoid weak setup and injury on low reps
some leg drive but keep elbow flexion
train the back, not a deadlift
